neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Cooperative but somewhat flat affect. MoCA 22/30 — loses 3 points on executive tasks (alternating trail, 1-letter fluency), 2 on delayed recall, 2 on abstraction. Digit span forward 6, backward 3 (reduced). Verbal fluency (F-words in 1 min): 7 (low normal cutoff 12). Clock drawing: poor planning, numbers crowded in right half.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. No saccadic intrusions. No primitive reflexes on cranial nerve exam.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone. Strength 5/5 throughout. No tremor. No rigidity. Bilateral palmomental reflex present. Snout reflex present. Grasp reflex absent.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric throughout. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffman.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact finger-nose, heel-shin. Normal rapid alternating movements.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal cadence, stride, and arm swing. No parkinsonian features. Tandem gait intact.
neurological_exam.additional: Wife reports: over the past 12 months, Mr. D has become 'a different person.' He no longer initiates conversations with grandchildren, has made several socially inappropriate comments to neighbors (remarked loudly on a neighbor's weight gain), has developed a fixation on watching the same two cowboy movies repeatedly, and has stopped maintaining personal hygiene without prompting. He recently impulsively spent $4,000 on a coin collection without discussing it with his wife. He denies any memory problems and dismisses his wife's concerns. Frontal release signs (bilateral palmomental, snout) present — indicating frontal lobe dysfunction.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive personality change and social withdrawal — 12 months (reported by wife)
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. D is a 64-year-old retired high school principal brought in by his wife of 38 years, who is the primary historian. She describes a gradual but unmistakable change in her husband's personality over approximately 12 months that began insidiously, with no clear precipitant. He was formerly a warm, socially engaged man who was beloved by his students and staff. Over the past year, he has become emotionally flat, rarely initiating conversation with family members and showing minimal interest in grandchildren who visit regularly. His wife notes that he has lost his usual warmth and empathy — when she cried during a sad film, he laughed. He has developed repetitive behaviors: he watches the same two Western films on a daily loop, eating exactly the same meal (a specific brand of macaroni and cheese) for lunch every day, and arranging his wallet contents in the same sequence each morning. He made an unprompted $4,000 online purchase of a coin collection without telling his wife, despite never having had interest in coins. He has made several socially disinhibited remarks in public. His memory for recent events appears relatively intact — he correctly recalls what he had for breakfast and what they watched the previous evening. He has no trouble with basic activities of daily living when prompted, but shows reduced initiation. There has been no acute change, no falls, no hallucinations, no seizures, and no prominent language difficulty. He retired from school administration 12 months ago, and his wife initially attributed the changes to post-retirement adjustment. Family history is notable for his father dying of possible dementia in his early 70s. His psychiatrist, seen 4 months ago, diagnosed him with late-onset depression and started him on sertraline, which he recently discontinued after 3 months with no improvement in his wife's estimation. He now presents to the neurology clinic at his wife's insistence.

findings.finding: Asymmetric hypometabolism involving bilateral frontal lobes, RIGHT greater than left. Right superior and middle frontal gyri show 18-22% reduction in FDG uptake compared to cerebellar reference. Left frontal involvement is milder (8-12% reduction). Right orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex also hypometabolic.
Mild bilateral anterior temporal hypometabolism, right greater than left. Right temporal tip shows 14% reduction. Mild right anterior temporal involvement.
Preserved — posterior cingulate cortex, precuneus, parietal association cortex, and occipital lobes show normal FDG uptake.
Caudate nuclei show mildly reduced FDG uptake bilaterally, right slightly more than left.

output.impression: Asymmetric right frontotemporal hypometabolism with relative preservation of posterior cortex — a pattern consistent with frontotemporal hypometabolism. Posterior cingulate and precuneus uptake are preserved. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.finding: NEGATIVE for amyloid plaque burden. No significant cortical amyloid deposition. SUVr values in all neocortical regions are below the established positivity threshold (SUVr <1.10 for florbetapir).

output.impression: Negative — sparse-to-no amyloid neuritic plaque density. No cortical amyloid deposition detected. Clinical correlation recommended.

FTD_Genetic_Panel.value: No pathogenic variant identified — heterozygous common variant c.1414C>T (rs5848) present but this is a common polymorphism, NOT pathogenic
No pathogenic variant identified — H1/H1 haplotype (common haplotype associated with slightly elevated PSP/CBD risk but not causative)

findings.finding: Executive function (DKEFS Trails, Color-Word Interference): Severely impaired. DKEFS Trails condition 4 (switching) score: 2nd percentile. Color-word inhibition: 4th percentile.
Verbal fluency: Letter fluency (FAS): 18 total (18th percentile — low average). Category fluency (animals): 11 (20th percentile). Borderline low — less severely impaired than letter fluency.

Episodic memory (HVLT-R): Immediate recall 7/12 trials 1-3 (30th percentile — low average). Delayed recall 5/12 (25th percentile). Recognition: 11/12 (50th percentile). Memory impairment is present but NOT severe — recognition is relatively preserved.
Working memory (WAIS-IV digit span): Forward 6, backward 3 — low average.

Social cognition (Reading the Mind in the Eyes, Faux Pas Test): Eyes test 18/36 (severely impaired, <5th percentile). Faux Pas: identifies only 3/10 faux pas scenarios (severely impaired). SEVERELY IMPAIRED social cognition — a cardinal feature of bvFTD.
Behavioral rating scales (informant — wife): FBI (Frontal Behavioral Inventory): 28/72 — elevated, indicating disinhibition, perseveration, and apathy.

output.impression: Neuropsychological profile consistent with probable behavioral-variant FTD: severely impaired executive function and social cognition with relative preservation of visuospatial function. Episodic memory mildly impaired; recognition relatively preserved. FBI score elevated, confirming significant frontal behavioral changes per informant. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.proposed: Review prior sertraline trial; consider appropriate symptomatic management for bvFTD behavioral symptoms
interactions: Sertraline + amlodipine: minimal clinical interaction — no adjustment needed
Note: SSRIs (sertraline, fluvoxamine) may modestly reduce disinhibition and perseverative behaviors in bvFTD — some evidence for modest benefit
contraindications: Avoid antipsychotics with strong anticholinergic properties (olanzapine, quetiapine at high doses) — can worsen cognitive function in FTD
Avoid cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) in bvFTD — NOT indicated; may worsen behavioral symptoms and agitation (evidence for harm in FTD)
warnings: No FDA-approved disease-modifying therapy for bvFTD currently available
Cholinesterase inhibitors are indicated for Alzheimer's disease but are CONTRAINDICATED in FTD — critical prescribing distinction
Low-dose SSRI (sertraline 50-100 mg or fluvoxamine) may help disinhibition and compulsive behaviors
Trazodone 50-300 mg at bedtime may help sleep and agitation in FTD
output.formulary_status: No disease-modifying therapy available for FTLD
alternatives: Trazodone 50-150 mg for behavioral disturbance and sleep

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) — sporadic, 5 of 6 Rascovsky diagnostic criteria met (disinhibition, apathy/inertia, loss of empathy, perseverative/stereotyped behaviors, executive neuropsychological deficit), supported by frontal atrophy on MRI, frontotemporal hypometabolism on FDG-PET, and negative amyloid PET

differential.key_features: No response to 3 months of sertraline; MoCA 22 with severe executive impairment; frontal atrophy and frontotemporal FDG-PET hypometabolism; severely impaired social cognition on formal testing — depression does not produce frontal atrophy or frontotemporal FDG-PET hypometabolism
Amyloid PET negative; normal CSF Abeta42 and p-tau; FDG-PET posterior cingulate sign absent; hippocampal volumes preserved; atrophy pattern frontal > temporal (AD shows hippocampal > frontal)
No gait apraxia, no urinary incontinence; ventriculomegaly proportionate to atrophy (not disproportionate); no periventricular lucency; triad of NPH not present

Only Fazekas 1 white matter changes — insufficient to cause behavioral syndrome of this severity; FDG-PET shows metabolic changes beyond what is expected from Fazekas 1 white matter disease; behavioral features (disinhibition, social cognition loss) more typical of FTLD

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mild to moderate bifrontal atrophy right > left; relatively preserved posterior cortex and hippocampus

optimal_actions.action: Standard dementia labs — exclude reversible causes (TSH, B12, RPR, HIV, copper)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: All normal — no reversible cause identified

optimal_actions.action: FDG-PET brain — characterize metabolic pattern (frontotemporal vs posterior)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Asymmetric right frontotemporal hypometabolism; absent posterior cingulate sign

optimal_actions.action: Amyloid PET — definitively exclude Alzheimer's pathology
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Negative — no cortical amyloid deposition; AD excluded

optimal_actions.action: Comprehensive neuropsychological testing — characterize cognitive profile
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Severely impaired executive function and social cognition; relatively preserved visuospatial; bvFTD profile

optimal_actions.action: FTD genetic panel — C9orf72, GRN, MAPT (given possible family history)

critical_actions: FDG-PET is essential — distinguishes FTD (frontal hypometabolism) from AD (posterior cingulate/parietal hypometabolism)
Amyloid PET or CSF Abeta42/p-tau MUST be obtained to exclude Alzheimer's pathology before finalizing bvFTD diagnosis
Do NOT prescribe cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) — contraindicated in FTD, may worsen symptoms
Apply Rascovsky 2011 criteria systematically: need 3 of 6 behavioral features for 'probable bvFTD'
contraindicated_actions: Prescribing cholinesterase inhibitors — not indicated in FTD, may worsen behavioral symptoms
Treating as depression without comprehensive neurocognitive evaluation — sertraline is appropriate trial but should not delay neurological workup if no response
Diagnosing bvFTD without amyloid exclusion — AD must be excluded before FTD diagnosis
key_reasoning_points: The ABSENCE of posterior cingulate hypometabolism on FDG-PET is the key discriminating feature from Alzheimer's disease — Alzheimer's invariably shows posterior cingulate and precuneus hypometabolism
Social cognition is severely impaired in bvFTD (Reading the Mind in the Eyes, Faux Pas) while visuospatial function is preserved — the opposite of Alzheimer's disease
Cholinesterase inhibitors are CONTRAINDICATED in FTD despite being standard of care for AD — frontotemporal lobar degeneration is not a cholinergic deficit syndrome

The clinically important difficulty of this case is the overlapping presentation with depression — behavioral withdrawal, apathy, and emotional blunting can appear in both; the frontal release signs, severely impaired social cognition, and neuroimaging distinguish them

red_herrings.data_point: Prior psychiatric diagnosis of late-onset depression
red_herrings.intended_effect: Accept psychiatric attribution and defer neurological workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Failed SSRI trial, absent posterior cingulate sign on FDG-PET, frontal atrophy, and severely impaired social cognition establish bvFTD over depression

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute behavioral syndrome to vascular/white matter disease
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fazekas 1 is mild and expected with vascular risk factors; insufficient to cause severe behavioral syndrome; FDG-PET metabolic changes are primary

metadata.notes: Moderate bvFTD — 64-year-old with 1-year personality change, prior psychiatric attribution. Asymmetric right frontotemporal hypometabolism on FDG-PET, absent posterior cingulate sign. Amyloid PET negative. Key teaching: cholinesterase inhibitors contraindicated in FTD.
